title: Target slice and direct algebraic bounds

add.label: Direct ledger
add.name: Generic bound
add.statement: Under (P5), E(2Q+2) ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ for every integer 0 ≤ Q < 2^λ.
add.proof: The coefficient of u² in E is (θ+ε_f)/2+9ε_f/2 ≥ 0, so E is convex. By (P5) its values at 2 and 2^{λ+1} are at most 2^{-λ} and 1, respectively. The affine function u/2^{λ+1} has exactly these endpoint values, so it bounds E from above on the interval by convexity. Set u=2Q+2.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct range
add.name: Search range
add.statement: For either sampler and its corresponding center c_w in the linked definition, let w be binary with w_0=1 and put k=1+wt(w). Throughout the support |r(w)−c_w|≤B. The second moment of r(w)−c_w is at most (g√(k/12)+1/2)² for independent coordinates and (g√((N+4)/48)+3/2)² for the centered sampler.
add.proof: Put m=(g+3)/2 and let Y denote a uniform draw from {2,…,g+1} minus m. Summing (j−(g−1)/2)² over 0≤j<g gives Var(Y)=(g²−1)/12, and |Y|≤(g−1)/2. For a sum Z of independent copies with real coefficients a_i and any rounding error of magnitude ≤b, the pointwise bound is (g−1)Σ|a_i|/2+b and the L² bound is g√(Σa_i²/12)+b, by the triangle inequality and independence. In the independent sampler the deviation has k coefficients 1 and rounding error km−⌊km⌋≤1/2 because 2km is integral. In the centered sampler the identity −⌊s/2⌋=−s/2+(s/2−⌊s/2⌋), for s=Σr_i over 1≤i≤N, gives coefficients 1 on the star draw and w_i−1/2 on the others. The rounding error is the sum of s/2−⌊s/2⌋ and the fractional part of the unrounded center, hence is ≤3/2. The coefficient norms give the stated squared L² bounds. The pointwise bounds are k(g−1)/2+1/2 and (N+2)(g−1)/4+3/2, each at most (N+1)(g+1)=B.

add.label: Direct gp-rank
add.name: Rank bound
add.statement: For either sampler and every stack W of rank d, gp(W)≤g^{−d}. For every v in its row space, gp(vᵀ)≥gp(W).
add.proof: Stack the rows as M. If its column 0 is nonzero, include that column in a column basis; otherwise omit it. Once the coordinates outside that basis are fixed, the equation Mr=u determines the pivot coordinates uniquely modulo q. If 0 is outside the basis, it need not be conditioned on, since it has zero column. The positive-index pivots each hit their prescribed values with independent probability 1/g or zero, and if 0 is a pivot its conditional probability given all positive indices is at most 1/g. Thus each fiber has probability ≤g^{−d}. Since vᵀr is a linear image of Mr, the largest fiber of Mr maps to one value of vᵀr, giving the other inequality.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct qap
add.name: QAP criterion
add.statement:
For any admissible evaluation points and symmetric W, passage is equivalent to each of the identities
P_W−W_{00} L_ρ=h Z(X−ρ)+Z_0 R,
P_W=h′ Z+Z_0 R,
when the remainder R is allowed. In either identity the remainder is R_W, the interpolant of degree below ν n_c of P_W/Z_0 on the cosets; the quotients have deg h<D−1 and deg h′<D. For a witness these identities apply to wwᵀ with W_{00}=1.
add.proof: For either identity, evaluation on the cosets forces R=R_W because Z vanishes there and Z_0 does not. The sums of its values there are the constraint tests by the QAP table. For exponents divisible by ν, the matrix of coset sums is ν times the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct νth powers of the coset representatives; the other exponents give zero. With no cosets the allowed remainder is zero and there are no constraint tests. Otherwise invertibility makes the constraint tests equivalent to R_W being allowed. Subtract Z_0 R_W from P_W. On the roots of Z the difference vanishes except possibly at d_j for 1≤j≤N, where its values are the Booleanity tests. Subtracting W_{00}L_ρ adds the root ρ without changing those values. Hence divisibility by the respective vanishing polynomials is equivalent to the remaining tests. The numerators have degree ≤2D−2 since Z_0 R_W and L_ρ have degree ≤D−1, so division by polynomials of degrees D and D−1 yields the claimed bounds. A witness passes the tests by its defining equations.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct classification
add.name: Classification
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack with row space of dimension at most three and no kernel vector has a witness in its row space.
add.proof:
Work over K=F_{q^n}. Let U have an F_q-basis of the row space as columns, d its column count, u_j the transpose of its row j, and h_s=Uᵀσ^s(z). No kernel vector means the entries of h_0 are F_q-independent. For s=a,b,c with a=n/2−1,b=n/2,c=n/2+1, assemble W_s from the U-weight coefficients, V-weight coefficients, and the σ^c conjugate of the U assembly, respectively. These have a unique expression W_s=UM_sUᵀ with M_s symmetric: applying a left inverse of U on both sides gives M_s, and the row and column spaces ensure the reconstruction. The ties imply M_s h_t=M_t h_s. The first d of these h_s are independent: a relation with coefficients λ_j would give the nonzero q-linear polynomial Σ_{j<d} λ_j X^{q^j} vanishing on all entries of h_a, hence on their F_q-span of q^d elements. Frobenius preserves their independence and the polynomial has degree at most q^{d−1}, a contradiction. Thus the h_s span K^d. Thus h_s↦M_s extends linearly, since any relation Σ_s λ_s h_s=0 gives (Σ_s λ_s M_s)h_t=0 for every t. Its trilinear form T(h,u,v)=uᵀM(h)v is symmetric by matrix symmetry and the ties on spanning arguments. The tests give T(h,u_j,u_j−u_0)=0 for every h, by linearity from h_s. Writing M_s for M(h_s), we have M_a=σ^a(M_c) and M_b=σ^b(M_b) by the conjugacy and even-degree V assembly.
If u_0=0, choose d of the u_j as a basis. T vanishes on basis triples with repetitions, so can be nonzero only for d=3, with one independent value t on the triples of distinct indices. In those basis coordinates the off-diagonal evaluations of M_s are t times the three coordinates of h_s. The two conjugacy identities, using σ^a(h_c)=σ^b(h_b)=h_0 and the basis over F_q, imply t h_a=σ^a(t)h_0 and t h_b=σ^b(t)h_0. The spanning condition for three vectors in dimension three rules out both h_a,h_b proportional to h_0. Thus t=0, and T=0 would make the stack zero.
With u_0≠0, complete it to a basis u_0,l_1,…,l_{d−1} from the rows. For each binary tuple δ of length d−1 let p_δ be the dual-coordinate vector taking values 1,δ_1,…,δ_{d−1} on this basis, and write w_δ=Up_δ and z_δ=z(w_δ)≠0. The test relations replace each repeated nonzero index of a basis triple by index 0 until distinct; symmetry then makes each triple's value depend only on its set A of nonzero indices. The cubes (hᵀp_δ)(uᵀp_δ)(vᵀp_δ) have entries ∏_{j∈A}δ_j on these triples. The matrix of these entries, indexing tuples by their support B, is the subset incidence matrix 1_{A⊆B}, triangular with unit diagonal under cardinality order. Hence T is a linear combination of these cubes with coefficients c_δ∈K. Pairs also realize all subsets A since d−1≤2; the same matrix proves independence of the squares p_δp_δᵀ.
It follows that M_s=Σ_δ c_δ σ^s(z_δ)p_δp_δᵀ. Comparing square coefficients in the two conjugacy identities shows c_δ/z_δ fixed by σ^a and σ^b, hence by σ since b−a=1. Write χ_δ=c_δ/z_δ∈F_q. Now take any linear passage test L over F_q. It vanishes on every W_s by vanishing on the stack coefficients. Consequently h_0ᵀQh_s=0, where Q=Σ_δ χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)p_δp_δᵀ is over F_q. Spanning gives h_0ᵀQ=0, and F_q-independence of the entries of h_0 gives Q=0. Independence of the squares gives χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)=0 for each δ. Some χ_δ is nonzero, since otherwise all assemblies and thus the stack vanish. The corresponding w_δ has coordinate 0 equal to 1 and its moment matrix passes every test, hence it is a witness.

add.label: Direct half
add.name: Factor one half
add.statement: In the experiment of Definition 3.6, $\Pr[\, b' = b \wedge \mathsf{Fail} \,] \le \frac12 + \frac14 (f_0 + f_1)$.
add.proof: Fix the shared coins in the uniform-masked-message game. By the coupling, either both bits lead to a target query or neither does; off the target event the same output guesses at most one bit correctly. Hence, putting p=Pr[Tgt], the off-target contribution to success with failure is at most (1−p)/2. On target it is at most f=(f_0+f_1)/2≤p, the probability of target with failure. Their sum is ≤1/2+f/2.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct inverse
add.name: Inverse theorem
add.statement: Under (I1)–(I6) in the linked inverse conditions, every nonzero v∈F_q^{N+1} with v_0=0 and gp(vᵀ)>θ has a short multiple x with x_0=0.
add.proof:
Write ε=ε_tr and μ=μ_tr. All box coordinates are independent and uniform on {2,…,g+1}. A fiber of a rank-e lattice fixes e coordinates after the others are specified, by an invertible row minor of its basis. Its density is at most g^{−e}.

Trimming. For a lattice Θ of rank 1≤d≤3 with basis B, a centered box coordinate has moment generating function sinh(gt/2)/(g sinh(t/2)) by a geometric sum, with limit 1 at zero. Since sinh(x)/x≥1 and (2j+1)!≥6^jj!, this is at most exp(g²t²/24). Thus the centered image Y=Bᵀr_I−y_Θ satisfies E e^{uᵀY}≤e^{uᵀΣ_Θu/2} by independence. For Z=Σ_Θ^{−1/2}Y and an independent standard Gaussian G in dimension d, integrate e^{√(99/100)GᵀZ} in either order: E e^{99‖Z‖²/200}≤E e^{99‖G‖²/200}=10^d. Markov's inequality and (I2) bound the mass removed by 10^d e^{−99R_tr²/200}≤ε.

Integral facts. For rows J of a largest minor, Cramer's rule makes each entry of B_iB_J^{−1} a ratio of a maximal minor to det B_J, hence at most one in magnitude. Thus restriction to J is injective on the span, and ‖y‖_∞≤‖y_J‖₁ there. For saturated Θ a unimodular extension of B gives an integral left inverse, so Bᵀ is onto the integer codomain. If Δ has rank k and all its k-minors have magnitude <q, some nonzero one survives reduction. In Smith form UΔV=S the k nonzero entries are therefore units mod q. If cᵀΔ≡0, the first k entries of cᵀU^{−1} are multiples of q. Set them to zero and multiply by U. This gives an integral relation reducing to cᵀ.

Prefixes. Put J first for a saturated rank-d Θ. Let B_k be the first k rows, d≤k≤|I|, and write B_k=Y_kC_k with Y_k a basis of the integer points of its span and C_k integral. These prefix lattices have rank d and largest minor J. If h_k,m_k are height and maximum fiber mass, then h_k[Z^d:B_kᵀZ^k]=h(Θ): the index is |det C_k| by transpose surjectivity, and minors scale by that determinant. The first prefix is Z^d, with h_d=1 and m_d=g^{−d}; the last is Θ. Adding a row enlarges the transpose image by a cyclic quotient of order s_k=h_{k+1}/h_k. The new coordinate must lie in one class mod s_k in a fiber, and B_kᵀ and Y_kᵀ have the same fibers by invertibility of C_k. Thus m_{k+1}≤m_k⌈g/s_k⌉/g≤m_k, and s_k≥g fixes the new coordinate.
For s=s_k<g we have m_{k+1}^b h_{k+1}^{b−1}≤m_k^b h_k^{b−1}. For s=1 this is monotonicity. Otherwise ⌈g/s⌉/g≤(1+s/g)/s≤s^{−1+1/b}. The last inequality holds for s≥2^b since 1+s/g≤2, and for 2≤s≤2^b by concavity of s^{1/b}−1−s/2^b and g≥2^b. The concave function is zero at 2^b and positive at 2 by ln(2)/b>2^{1−b} for b≥7 (true at 7, with b/2^{b−1} decreasing).
For rank three, the r ratios above one multiply to h=h(Θ). The upper density factor ∏(1/s_k+1/g) over these ratios exceeds 1/h by at most r(1/2+1/g)^{r−1}/g, by telescoping one factor at a time. If r=0 this error is zero; otherwise the bound is maximal at r=2, since the successive ratio after that is (1+1/r)(1/2+1/g)<1. Therefore m(Θ)≤g^{−3}ξ_tr(1/h+1/g). If m(Θ)≥μ, solving for h gives h≤H_3 by (I2); then m(Θ)h≤Γ_3/g³ by (I4).

Image count. Let Θ of rank d∈{1,2,3} on |I|≤N trim a nonempty box set F on I and a new index i′. Each point of its image Φ(F) under Φ(r)=(Bᵀr_I,r_{i′}) has mass at most m(Θ)/g. We need two cases. In the full-dimensional case the image lies in an index-q coset. Set k=d+1, δ=q, J=∅ and B_2=B, with the empty minor assigned determinant 1. In the other case F^⊥ has rank 1≤d′<d, a largest minor J⊆I and restrictions to I in the span of Θ. For its basis Y, Y_J is invertible, so B_J has rank d′. Extend the saturated integral kernel basis of B_J to a unimodular basis of Z^d, with kernel columns last. This changes B to (B_1,B_2) with (B_2)_J=0 and (B_1)_J invertible. Trimming is invariant under this change; form Φ with the new B. The transpose map (a,t)↦(Ba,t) identifies the image's real normal space with that of F by the restriction hypothesis, so k=dim Φ(F)=d+1−d′. Split a basis V of its saturated normal lattice into the first d′ rows V_1 and remaining k rows V_2. Pulling back integral normals gives (B_1)_JV_1=Y_JC for integral nonsingular C, so |det(B_1)_J|·|det V_1|≥h(F^⊥). Dropping the first d′ image coordinates is injective on differences in ker Vᵀ. The projected differences satisfy V_2ᵀx=0 mod V_1ᵀZ^{d′}, a subgroup of index δ=|det V_1| by transpose surjectivity. Use the identity projection in the full-dimensional case.
In both cases the projected convex hull has dimension k in an index-δ coset, so a simplex of its lattice vertices has volume ≥δ/k!. The lattice point bound gives count ≤k!·vol/δ+k≤(k+1)!·vol/δ. The hull lies in an interval of length ≤g times the projected ellipsoid. For j=k−1, that ellipsoid has volume vol(Ball_j)(gR_tr/√12)^j√det(B_2ᵀB_2) by the singular values of its linear map, with Ball_j the Euclidean unit ball. By Cauchy–Binet and (B_2)_J=0, multiplying the square root by |det(B_1)_J| bounds it by h(Θ)√binom(N,j): each block minor is a maximal minor of B. Using binom(N,j)≤N^j/j!, the resulting bound is
Pr[F]·δ·|det(B_1)_J|≤m(Θ)h(Θ)g^j R_tr^j N^{j/2}(j+2)!vol(Ball_j)/√(12^j j!).
The last factor is 2√3, √2π or 20π/(9√2) for j=1,2,3. By (I3) this gives Pr[F]≤Λ_d g^d h(Θ)m(Θ)/q in the first case and Pr[F]h(F^⊥)≤Λ_{d−d′}g^{d−d′}h(Θ)m(Θ) in the second.

Regularization. Suppose saturated Θ on at most N indices has rank d∈{1,2,3} and m(Θ)≥μ+(3−d)ε. We find a regular saturated extension of rank ≤3 losing at most (3−d)ε. Induct downward from the rank-three prefix bound. For d≤2, choose a largest fiber in each prefix, then trim it by R_{k−1} if such a lattice was constructed, obtaining F_k. Then Pr[F_k]≥m_k−ε≥μ+(2−d)ε. Its normal lattice contains Θ_k. If it is larger, its rank e is in [d+1,3] by saturation and Pr[F_k]>g^{−4}. Its density meets μ+(3−e)ε, so induction constructs the regular extension R_k with m(R_k)≥m_k−(3−d)ε. At the final prefix this proves the result if R_k exists.
Otherwise let j be the last prefix with R_j, or d−1. After j+1 the ratios are <g: a ratio ≥g fixes the new coordinate, whose unit vector would be in the normal lattice Θ_{k+1} and vanish on J. Hence m_k(m_kh_k)^{b−1} is nonincreasing from j+1. To prove regularity of Θ it suffices to bound this product there by μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1}. If j=d−1 this is g^{−db}≤μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1} by (I4). Otherwise F_{j+1} is trimmed by R_j of rank e>d and has normal lattice Θ_{j+1}, largest minor J in the old prefix and restrictions in span(Θ_j)⊆span(R_j). The second image bound and regularity of R_j give Pr[F_{j+1}]h_{j+1}≤Λ_{e−d}Γ_e/g^d. By (I4), m_{j+1}≤A_inv Pr[F_{j+1}], while m_{j+1}≤m_j≤Pr[F_j]+ε≤g^{−d−1}+ε≤μP_d^{b−1}. Multiplying m_{j+1} by the bound for (m_{j+1}h_{j+1})^{b−1} gives the desired product by A_inv Λ_{e−d}Γ_e P_d≤Γ_d.

Support induction. Relabel to put the m nonzero positive coordinates first. Conditioning on added independent summands shows that each nonempty prefix has guessing probability ≥gp(vᵀ)>θ; conditioning on all but one nonzero coordinate bounds it by 1/g. Maintain a regular saturated Θ of rank d≤3 whose reduction contains v_{[i]} and with density at least gp(v_{[i]}ᵀ)−3ε>μ. For i=1 use Z, onto modulo q, with h=1 and m(Θ)=1/g. This is regular since (I4) and μ<1/g give Γ_1≥1. For all prefixes h≤H_d by regularity (d≤2) or the rank-three bound.
On a largest minor the lattice determinant is h. The ℓ₁ ball has volume 2^d/d!, so the successive minima product is ≤d!h. Mahler's basis lengths are at most λ₁, λ₂ and 3λ₃/2 for the successive minima present. The projected ℓ₁ lengths bound the lifted ℓ∞ norms. Thus choose B with ∏‖B_j‖_∞≤a_d h, a_d=1,2,9 respectively. Set v_{[i]}≡Bc′, c=(c′,v_{i+1}) and trim a largest modular fiber cᵀΦ=t. The result F has density ≥gp(v_{[i+1]}ᵀ)−ε>μ. Its image lies in an index-q coset because v_{i+1}≠0. Full dimension would force Pr[F]≤Λ_dΓ_d/q<μ by the image bound and (I5).
For the difference matrix Δ of the image, rank k≤d, the j-th moment row has entries bounded by 2R_tr√[(Σ_Θ)_{jj}]≤T_tr‖B_j‖_∞ by Cauchy–Schwarz. The new-coordinate row is bounded by g−1≤T_tr. Each bound is at least one if we use T_tr for the last row. Thus the k-minors are bounded by d!T_tr^d∏‖B_j‖_∞≤d!a_d H_dT_tr^d<q by (I5). Since cᵀΔ≡0, lift c integrally and pull it back by Φᵀ to a member of F^⊥ reducing to v_{[i+1]}. This normal lattice has positive rank, at most three by the fiber bound, and m(F^⊥)≥Pr[F]>θ−ε≥μ+2ε. Its regular extension loses ≤2ε, giving the next prefix.
At i=m take Bz_0≡v_{[m]}≠0. The inverse image of the line of z_0 modulo q has index q^{d−1}, and its dominant-minor projection has determinant h q^{d−1}. By (I6) and integrality of h, d!h q^{d−1}≤β^d. The ℓ₁ ball of radius β reaches Minkowski's volume threshold, so shrinking to equality if needed gives a nonzero projected point B_Jz. Lift back to 0<‖Bz‖_∞≤‖B_Jz‖₁≤β<q. Thus its residue is a nonzero multiple of the prefix, and zero padding and inverse relabeling give the result with x_0=0.

add.label: Direct efficiency
add.name: Efficiency
add.statement:
For Praxis as specified in Appendix A, with the evaluation points placed in $\mathcal{H}$ as in Section 4.4 and $n \le D$, and with $n_1 := (2K_1 + 1)(N+1) + \Delta + (\nu - 1)n_{\mathsf{c}}/J'$ and $n_2 := 6K_2 (N+1) + 3K_2 + \frac{3n}{2}(J + J') + 13n - 8$:

 
(a) \emph{Size.} A ciphertext consists of $n_1$ elements of $\mathbb{G}_1$, $2 n_2$ of $\mathbb{G}_2$, one of $\mathbb{G}_T$, the seed, and $\mu$ bits.
(b) \emph{Encryption.} $\mathsf{Enc}$ computes one scalar multiplication of a generator for each of these group elements and one more in $\mathbb{G}_T$.
(c) \emph{Decryption.} Outside the search in line (9) of Dec, $\mathsf{Dec}$ computes $18K_2 + 4J + 2J' + 2$ pairings; at most $(2K_1 + 1) N$ additions and MSMs (sums $\sum_{i \le s} a_i P_i$ of length $s$) of total length at most $3n + 2D + (\nu - 1)n_{\mathsf{c}}$ in $\mathbb{G}_1$; at most $12 K_2 N$ additions and MSMs of total length $3n\,(J + J') + 26n - 16$ in $\mathbb{G}_2$; and $18K_2 + 4J + 2J' + 1$ additions and four scalar multiplications in $\mathbb{G}_T$.
(d) \emph{Search.} The search in line (9) of Dec can be computed with $O(\sqrt{|t|} + 1)$ operations in $\mathbb{G}_T$, where $t$ is its result. On a ciphertext of $\mathsf{Enc}$, this is $O(\sqrt{g}\, N^{1/4})$ operations in expectation over the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$.
add.proof:
Let C=3n/2 be the number of cells. The published first-group blocks have sizes 2K_1(N+1), Δ, (ν−1)n_c/J′ and N+1. The second-group blocks per copy have sizes 6K_2(N+1), 3K_2, CJ, CJ′, 3(n−1), and 5(2n−1). The second-group block is doubled by α, and the sole published target element is [ακ]_T. Each published exponent takes one generator multiplication; the extra target multiplication is for [κ]_T. The seed and masked message have the stated sizes.
The first-group witness sums use (2K_1+1)N additions, initializing each with coordinate 0. The leg sums use 2K_1·3K_2=3n total MSM entries, and the quotient and remainder sums use at most 2D+(ν−1)n_c by their degree and coefficient support. The two second-group witness sums per leg and per sector use 12K_2 N additions in all. In one sector the weighted quotient bases use CJ MSM entries (both key and other together), the remainder bases use CJ′ and the cancellation bases use 13n−8, doubling to the stated count.
In one sector Λ uses 6K_2+2J+J′+1 pairings, and Ψ uses 3K_2. Their sums use two fewer additions than their total count, since each is nonempty. Both sectors plus the two target subtractions and one key subtraction give the stated target additions; forming the target and recovering K each use two scalar multiplications.
If the search base is zero, it returns zero for zero target and otherwise fails, with constant work. For nonzero base the interval contains at most one solution since its length is <q. Search consecutive centered intervals of radii 1,4,16,… capped at B, using the interval search bound. If t is the returned solution, the geometric series costs O(√|t|+1); without a solution it costs O(√B). On honest input a skipped search costs zero. Otherwise Λ′=(r(w)−c_w)Ψ^α by the combination identities, so the support bound gives t=r(w)−c_w for nonzero base, and t=0 for zero base. The expectation of √|r(w)−c_w| is at most the fourth root of its second moment, hence O(√g·N^{1/4}).

add.label: Direct lifting
add.name: Lifting by prefix spans
add.statement: For prime q, 2β<q and 24β⁴<q³, lifting a nonzero v∈F_q^{N+1} with v_0=0 returns a short multiple if one exists and ⊥ otherwise, deterministically in poly(N,log q) time.
add.proof:
Drop coordinate 0, permute and normalize v_1=1. In the prefix lattice L_i defined by x_j≡x_1v_j mod q, any four box points (|x_j|≤β) have each four-row minor divisible by q³ by column elimination modulo q. Its magnitude is ≤24β⁴<q³, so all such points span at most three dimensions.
Start with the empty prefix and store the bounded span S by a bounded basis. To extend to L_i use the rank-≤4 lattice L_i∩(S×R), which contains all bounded extensions. Express S by rational elimination on its stored points, clearing denominators. With integral slack z_j encode each congruence by x_j−x_1v_j=qz_j. For equation matrix A, top-first column Hermite form of [A;I] gives the kernel basis in the zero-top columns. Drop the unique slack.
In those ≤4 integer coordinates, impose the box inequalities. Find a point outside the current found span by testing each sign of an annihilator basis scaled to integer coefficients, using f≥1 or f≤−1. After at most three increases and one failure, store the points in prefix coordinates. Each stage uses polynomial bit inputs by bounded stored points, rational elimination and the Hermite bound. At the end a nonzero found point reduces nontrivially since β<q. Undo the permutation and restore zero at coordinate 0, or return ⊥ if none.

edges.demand: X^k sums over a coset of order ν to ν·δ^k if ν divides k, and to zero otherwise.
A convex body of affine dimension k holds at most k!·vol + k lattice points.
A basis of a saturated lattice extends to an ambient unimodular basis. Minkowski’s second theorem and Mahler’s basis bound give the basis norm product bounds h, 2h and 9h at ranks one, two and three.
A symmetric convex body of volume 2^d·det contains a nonzero lattice point: the short multiple.
